about: Two prayers the priest says for himself alone, and yet they run in the plural — “from us”, “our iniquities”, “that we may be counted worthy” — until the second closes on the singular: “all my sins”. Only one word of them is said aloud — Orémus; the rest nobody hears. “Sancta sanctórum” is a Hebrew superlative rendered word for word: holy of holies, the innermost place of the Temple. The second prayer speaks of relics that are here — the priest is at that moment kissing the altar, and every consecrated altar has relics sealed within it; the word “hic” therefore points at the very altar his lips touch.

s01.narrative: The priest spreads and rejoins his hands — the gesture that opens a prayer in the Roman rite — and says one word aloud.

s03.narrative: The priest goes up the steps toward the altar and says the rest under his breath, for himself alone.

s04.translation: Take away from us our iniquities, we beseech Thee, O Lord, that we may be worthy to enter the holy of holies with pure minds.

s06.narrative: With joined hands resting on the altar the priest bows over it and begins the second prayer.

s07.translation: We beseech Thee, O Lord, by the merits of Thy Saints,

s08.narrative: The priest kisses the altar in the middle — the altar the words of the prayer are speaking of.

s09.translation: whose relics are here, and of all the Saints: that Thou wouldst deign to forgive me all my sins. Amen.

w001.function: A hortatory subjunctive in the first person plural. The only word of this prayer said aloud; the rest goes silently.

w002.function: The imperative of an irregular verb compounded from fero: literally “carry off”.

w004.function: Ablative after “a” (w003). The priest speaks in the plural although he is praying for himself — the whole prayer keeps that number.

w005.function: Set into the very middle of the clause, between verb and object; it changes nothing in the structure and only softens the request.

w007.function: Accusative plural — the object of “Aufer” (w002). The bare form could also be nominative.

w009.function: It opens a purpose clause with the subjunctive: what the taking away is for.

w011.function: An adjective used as a noun, neuter plural: holy things. With “sanctórum” (w012) it forms a Hebrew superlative rendered word for word.

w012.function: A neuter genitive plural beside “Sancta” (w011): the holiness of holinesses — the innermost place of the Temple. The gender comes not from the form but from the fact that things, not persons, are meant.

w013.function: Agrees with “méntibus” (w015), though it stands well before it — Latin likes to hold an adjective and its noun apart.

w014.function: A deponent (passive form, active meaning); it governs the infinitive “introíre” (w016): that we may deserve to enter.

w015.function: Ablative of manner: in what disposition. Mens is thought and will rather than feeling.

w016.function: An infinitive depending on “mereámur” (w014). The same verb the priest used at the foot of the altar: I will go in unto the altar of God.

w018.function: Accusative after “Per” (w017) — through whom, by whose mediation. Almost every prayer of the Roman rite ends this way.

w019.function: Apposition to “Christum” (w018): the same case, because an apposition inherits the case of the noun it restates.

w022.function: Indicative, not subjunctive: “we pray”, not “let us pray”. One letter separates it from “Orémus” (w001).

w023.function: Accusative — the object of “Orámus” (w022): we beseech thee.

w026.function: Accusative plural after “per” (w025) — the ground on which the priest asks.

w027.function: An adjective used as a noun: holy persons. Unlike “Sancta” (w011), where the same word meant holy things.

w029.function: Genitive plural: the relics belong to them. The pronoun points back to “Sanctórum” (w027).

w030.function: Nominative, the subject of the relative clause: the relics are here, sealed in the altar the priest kisses as he says the words.

w031.function: An adverb of place — it points at the altar the priest is kissing at that moment.

w035.function: A second genitive depending on “mérita” (w026): the merits of those whose relics are here, and the merits of all the saints.

w036.function: It opens a purpose clause — what the priest is actually asking for.

w038.function: Subjunctive after “ut” (w036); the courtly turn of the Roman prayers — not “forgive” but “be pleased to forgive”.

w041.function: A singular possessor after a whole prayer spoken in the plural — the form itself is accusative plural, with “peccáta” (w040) — here at last the priest speaks for himself alone.
